prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B006 to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The Kane-Mele papers established that time-reversal symmetry together with spin-orbit coupling divides band insulators into two classes, with protected helical edge states in two dimensions as the physical consequence. That is a new classification of electronic matter, not a refinement of a known one. Molenkamp's HgTe quantum-well experiment then gave the unambiguous conductance signature that turned the prediction into an observed phase. The idea has been confirmed for almost two decades by transport, ARPES and STM, so maturity is not in doubt. Reading the full round-1 exchange, what persuades me is the structure of the argument and not the count: the chair is right that several moves followed colleagues' reasoning, and the support I weigh is that Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson each gave a concrete, checkable reason for theory plus first realisation as the selection principle. As the member who still works closest to quantum devices, I also note that the Z2 edge physics is of direct interest to those of us building circuits, and that this does not enter my judgment of the credit. On the chair's question about 2016: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz recognised topological transitions in 1D and 2D and the Chern-type invariants of broken time-reversal quantum Hall systems. The Z2 invariant with time-reversal symmetry intact, and a topological state in a nonmagnetic insulator with no applied field, is a different symmetry class with a different experimental realisation. Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig have stated that distinction clearly enough that my own round-1 concern about the increment is resolved, provided the citation says it.
statement.case_against: Three names cannot honour everyone with a substantial claim. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, and Zhang's death means it cannot be fully repaired by a later prize. Hasan's 3D ARPES observation and the 3D theory of Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy fall outside this configuration, and the citation as written is limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect so it does not imply that the 3D materials discovery is recognised. The 2016 prize still leaves some committee members with a reduced appetite for a second topological award, which I regard as a legitimate concern but not a scientific objection. Applications remain modest. Finally, a prize this contested on attribution invites the criticism that the committee simply chose the cleanest-looking slice of a larger story.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp after Mehlig's argument, and says he could still accept the Hasan version if colleagues find Mele's omission less costly.
responses.response: I am glad we have converged on the trio, and I also said I could live with the Hasan version, so I should be explicit about where I now stand. Your own point that the 3D priority question (Bi-Sb versus Bi2Se3, and theory preceding experiment) is the weakest consensus is the reason I no longer see Hasan replacing Mele as an improvement: it trades a clean co-authorship of the founding theory for a contested experimental priority. I would not accept the Hasan version over the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp one now. I agree with you that the Z2 invariant under preserved time-reversal symmetry is a different class from what the 2016 prize recognised, and I would write that into the citation wording.

responses.point: Eriksson moved his first choice from B017 to B006 on maturity arguments, keeps B017 as first alternative, and says the citation must state the distinction from the 2016 prize explicitly.
responses.response: I agree that the citation is a fairness instrument and should say plainly what is being recognised: the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall state of a time-reversal-invariant insulator, and the HgTe observation. That wording keeps the 3D story out by design and not by accident. On B017 I share your reading that the open question is timing and not concept; I gave weight to the unsettled pairing mechanism in round 1, and your statement that the phases are reproduced by many groups is fair, so I would call it a prize for a later year, not a rejected one. I do not rank it above B006 now.

responses.point: Kroll argues that magic-wavelength lattice trapping is a new principle, distinct from frequency combs (2005) and ion control (2012), that the pending redefinition of the second should not delay the prize, and that the B047 credit is the cleanest on the shortlist.
responses.response: The distinction you draw is persuasive: combs supply the readout, ion control is a different system, and magic-wavelength trapping removes the light-shift problem for a many-atom ensemble. That is a separate invention, and I withdraw the suggestion in my round-1 response that the adjacent prizes made B047 look like a refinement. I also agree the prize should not wait for the metrologists. My remaining difference is breadth of consequence across subfields, not quality, and I note that you rightly flag your own field proximity. On the chair's question about a two-part B006 plus B047 prize, I still cannot see a way to do it inside three people: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp plus Katori and Ye would be five, and shrinking B006 to two names would split the Kane-Mele discovery we have just agreed not to split.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B047 first, says strength of opening support is not an attribution we can defend, and worries the 2016 prize and the 2D/3D split reduce appetite for a second topological prize.
responses.response: You are right that B006's lead in opening rankings is not an argument, and I want to engage your attribution concern directly. If the citation is confined to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe observation, the contested 3D story is not claimed, and the remaining objection is the HgTe proposers, which is a cost shared by any trio. That is a real cost but it falls within the usual limits of a three-person cap. On 2016, I think the Z2 distinction is resolved by symmetry class and realisation. Our remaining disagreement is whether B047's cleaner attribution outweighs B006's broader scientific reach, and I place the latter ahead. I also accept your point about ion-clock groups as an adjacent claim for B047, and I list B047 as an alternative for that reason.

responses.point: Mehlig asked whether Johansson's connection to the superconducting-circuit community should be weighed when counting first-place support for B038, and argues the 3D case is partly carried by Kane and Mele through Fu-Kane-Mele.
responses.response: The question is fair and my answer is yes: my opening first place for B038 should be discounted, which is why I moved to B006 in round 1 and why B038 is only an alternative now. I disclose this again below. On the substance, your point that Hasan's claim is partly carried by the Fu-Kane-Mele theory is the strongest argument for keeping the trio as it is. I would add one qualification: citation wording should not imply that the 3D experimental discovery is being recognised, since the 3D theory credit does not cover the first observations.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, now adopts theory plus first realisation as the selection principle and asks whether the committee should judge the discovery and not the subject-area label.
responses.response: I agree with that principle and it is the reason I support the trio. Applied to B038, I would still hold my round-1 reservation that circuit QED is mostly an enabling architecture and that a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after 2025 needs an explicit distinction I cannot yet supply, with Girvin's omission as a separate attribution gap. I would not say it should never be recognised, and the committee should know I am the least neutral member on the question. In answer to your second question on IceCube, I have nothing to add beyond the AMANDA and collaboration-size concern, and I do not see B048 changing the outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts omitting Hasan and the HgTe proposers (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang), and whether the citation wording keeps the claim honestly limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect.
Whether the 2016 prize leaves enough room for a second topological award; I judge the Z2 distinction sufficient but others may weigh the subject-area overlap more heavily.

Whether optical lattice clocks (B047), now argued by Kroll and Lindroth as a distinct invention, should outrank B006 once breadth of consequence is weighed; I cannot test the metrology priority claims independently.
Whether B038 could be justified in a later year given the 2025 prize and Girvin's omission; I am the least neutral member on this point.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I direct WACQT at Chalmers, work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, and have documented ties to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and to the circuit-QED community; Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. This bears on B038, which I list only as an alternative, and my opening first place for it should be discounted, as Mehlig asked. Olsson shares an institution with me. I have no documented connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or the other credited names on B006 and B047, and my work on B031 is neighbouring field proximity only.
